clue.text: Operatic game

blocks.note: first meaning: a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera
second meaning: a card game for one player, called solitaire in America

explanation.walkthrough: 'Operatic' stands for the title of an opera, the 1881 Gilbert and Sullivan piece; Americans know the card game as solitaire.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both the Savoy opera satirising aesthetes and the single-player card game with a dealt-out layout.

clue.text: Rotten place to clear out

blocks.note: to place something is to put it
to rid a house of pests is to clear them out

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up a rotten, run-down place that needs clearing out.
explanation.definitionFit: Putrid food or flesh is decaying and foul-smelling, the plain sense of rotten.

clue.text: Jack, a man wearing canvas

blocks.note: a jack tar, or simply a tar, is a sailor
any man's name will do; here it is Paul
someone wearing a coat is in it

explanation.surface: A sailor and another man are dressed in canvas clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a man' is a crossword invitation to supply any male first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is a sheet of heavy waterproofed canvas used as a cover, so the material stands for it.

clue.text: Drawing level some time before nightfall

blocks.note: first meaning: making things equal, as when a team scores to tie
second meaning: the later part of the day as darkness approaches

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a match where the score is tied late in the day; read 'evening' as two syllables, then as even-ing.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb form it means making equal or squaring up; as a noun it is the period around dusk.

clue.text: Junction eight, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken word, so the spelling may differ from the sound

blocks.note: a rowing eight is a boat's crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: Someone hears a railway announcement about junction number eight.
explanation.walkthrough: CREWE is a town in Cheshire, England, famous as one of Britain's great railway junctions.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cheshire town grew up around a major railway interchange where several main lines meet.

clue.text: Specifically intended to cause an uprising

definitions.text: Specifically intended to cause an uprising

blocks.clueFragment: Specifically intended to cause an uprising
blocks.note: surface reading: a political plot designed to start a rebellion

blocks.clueFragment: Specifically intended to cause an uprising
blocks.note: setter's reading: a specific is a medicine, and this one makes the stomach contents rise

explanation.surface: A conspiracy has been engineered to provoke a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Specifically' hides the medical noun specific, a remedy for one purpose; the uprising is vomiting.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance given to induce vomiting, bringing the stomach's contents back up.

clue.text: During repast, Richard's oral examination

indicators.note: oral means spoken, so the name is taken by its sound rather than its spelling
something during a meal happens inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a repast is a meal
Dick is the familiar form of Richard, here spelt by sound

explanation.surface: Richard sits a spoken test over lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oral examination' looks like one phrase, but oral belongs to the wordplay and examination alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical is the everyday name for a physical check-up by a doctor, an examination of health.

clue.text: Vagrant parking under a car

indicators.note: in a down answer, being under something means sitting below it, so this piece is written second

blocks.note: a tram is a car running on rails, a tramcar
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A homeless person is found sheltering under a parked car.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'under' puts the parking letter below the car, so it comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tramp is a homeless wanderer with no settled home, the same as a vagrant.

clue.text: Such com comforts are material to

definitions.text: Such com comforts are material to

blocks.note: surface reading: a remark that bodily comforts matter to someone
setter's reading: such points at the missing word that completes the stock phrase ending in comforts
stray scan text with no part in the clue, a duplicated start of the next word

explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper scan repeats a fragment here: read it as 'Such comforts are material', a fill-in-the-blank clue for a familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Creature comforts are the physical pleasures of good food, warmth and a soft bed, which are purely material.

clue.text: He says he doesn't know 1 9 - it's interrupting the dance

blocks.note: surface reading: a man confessing ignorance of some fact
setter's reading: a man whose stated position is that the existence of God cannot be known
damaged scan text; no wordplay could be recovered from it, so it is left unexplained rather than guessed

explanation.walkthrough: The scan of this clue is garbled after the opening words; only the definition part can be read with confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnostic holds that whether any deity exists is unknowable, so professes no knowledge either way.

clue.text: Event for Manxmen?

blocks.note: surface reading: a sporting contest held on the Isle of Man
setter's reading: the emblem of the Isle of Man has three running legs, so a Manxman is jokingly given three

explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland, has as its symbol the triskelion, three armoured legs joined at the hip.
explanation.definitionFit: In this school sports-day contest two runners tie adjacent legs together, giving each pair three legs between them.

clue.text: One drink imbibed by Miss West in picture

indicators.note: what is imbibed is swallowed, so the drink ends up inside the name

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Mae West was the Hollywood actress
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: Mae West is shown in a film still drinking something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in picture' sounds like being in a film, Mae West's world, but picture is a verb meaning to form an image.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture something is to form a mental image of it, which is what imagining is.

clue.text: No small volume for one to place on the back of one's head!

blocks.note: O is nought, the same as no or nothing
cc, cubic centimetres, measures a small volume
I is the Roman numeral one
to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: Someone balances a book on the back of their head, though not a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a slim book perched behind one's head; the exclamation mark flags the oddity.
explanation.definitionFit: The occiput is the anatomical term for the rear part of the skull, the back of the head.

clue.text: Outrageous Jingoism?

definitions.note: read cryptically as a rant about the flag, a noun phrase

blocks.note: first meaning: shockingly obvious and offensive
second meaning, cryptic: split in two, the word is a tirade about the national banner

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals the whimsical second reading: jingoism is noisy patriotism, so it could be called a flag-rant.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagrant offence is glaring and shameless, so blatant that it outrages anyone who sees it.

clue.text: Rewriting a decent love story

indicators.note: rewriting something produces a new version, so the letters are set down in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: An author revises a romance to make it respectable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love story' reads as one phrase, a romance, but love only supplies a letter and story is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short personal story about an amusing or interesting incident.

clue.text: A flop who should change roles

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so these letters must take a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor who keeps failing ought to try different parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is someone who habitually fails, and a flop is a failure, whether person or show.

clue.text: With pretentious air, dog can cause a diversion

blocks.note: to put on side is to put on airs, behave pretentiously
to dog someone is to follow or track them

explanation.surface: A haughty dog can distract everyone around it.
explanation.walkthrough: Side is an old British slang word for swagger or pretension, as in 'no side about him'.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidetrack someone is to divert them from their main purpose, steering attention elsewhere.

clue.text: A doubter can be made impervious to persuasion

indicators.note: something that can be made is constructed from raw material, so these letters get rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sceptic can be turned into someone who will not listen to argument.
explanation.definitionFit: An obdurate person is stubbornly unyielding and refuses to change their mind whatever is said.

clue.text: Most of German town on the river Spree

indicators.note: most of something is all but a little of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: Bingen am Rhein is a wine town on the Rhine

explanation.surface: A German town stands on the banks of the Spree river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the river Spree' reads as Berlin's river, but the Spree is the definition and the town sits on the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: A binge is a bout of overindulgence in drink, food or spending, a spree.

clue.text: Upright means follow their justification

blocks.note: the proverb says the end justifies the means
means are ways of doing something

explanation.surface: An honest person's methods should be guided by their moral reasons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means follow' puts the means after their justification, which the proverb 'the end justifies the means' says is the end; the final S is the plural ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Something standing endways is placed on its end, vertical rather than lying flat, so upright.

clue.text: Prank ceased being funny when Father came in

indicators.note: something funny is odd or peculiar, so these letters behave strangely and shift about
coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: The children's practical joke stopped being amusing once Dad walked in.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a reckless or mischievous adventure, a piece of daring fun like a prank.

clue.text: Calm sea

definitions.note: the ocean's name, a proper noun

blocks.note: first meaning: peaceful, peace-loving
second meaning: the largest ocean, named for its gentleness

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a weather report, 'calm sea'; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacific means peaceable or tranquil, and Magellan gave that name to the great ocean.

clue.text: Secret's out, forsooth!

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are set out of place

blocks.note: taken as written, its letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in old-fashioned English that the secret has leaked.
explanation.definitionFit: Certes is an archaic word for certainly or truly, just as old as forsooth, which means indeed.

clue.text: Between girl and boy, I would be helpless

indicators.note: between two people means flanked by them, so one piece sits inside the pair

blocks.note: Una is a girl's name
Ed is a boy's name
I'd is the contraction of I would

explanation.surface: Someone stuck between a girl and a boy feels unable to act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'helpless' is a stretch: it means without help, as in alone, rather than powerless.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaided means without assistance from anyone, the literal sense of help-less.

clue.text: Old boot a sound cover

indicators.note: a sound is what you hear, so the word is chosen by how it is spoken

blocks.note: taken as written
a veil covers the face

explanation.surface: A worn-out shoe makes a decent covering.
explanation.walkthrough: Boot is an old verb meaning to profit or help, as in 'what boots it?', and avail means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail is to be of use or benefit, the sense of the archaic verb to boot.

clue.text: Connecting link and chain as an accessory

blocks.note: a neck of land is a narrow strip connecting two larger areas
to chain something up is to tie it

explanation.surface: A jeweller offers links and a chain as fashion extras.
explanation.definitionFit: A necktie is worn knotted at the collar as a finishing item of dress, a man's accessory.

clue.text: Girl with money out of the ordinary

indicators.note: something taken out of a word is removed from it, leaving the rest

blocks.note: L stands for pound, the British money unit
normal means ordinary

explanation.surface: A girl with unusual wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of the ordinary' looks like a phrase meaning unusual, but out of is the removal and the ordinary gives the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a woman's first name, and girl in crosswords invites any female name.

clue.text: Actually, a man engaged in diplomacy holds sovereign off

indicators.note: something that holds another has it inside, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Sam is a man's name
someone at work is engaged in it
tact is diplomacy
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diplomat keeps a monarch at a distance.
explanation.walkthrough: Diplomacy wraps around both the sovereign and off, so it is split in two with the other pieces in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Used to introduce a plain truth, the four-word phrase means in reality or in fact.

clue.text: Engage to listen out

indicators.note: out here means put out of place, so these letters fall into another order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes on a person to hear complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist recruits or helpers is to engage them, enrolling them into service.

clue.text: Lands a plane - on Shrove Tuesday

definitions.note: a time phrase standing for what is eaten then, the plural noun

blocks.note: first meaning: brings an aircraft down flat, dropping vertically
second meaning: the thin batter dishes eaten on that day

explanation.walkthrough: Shrove Tuesday, the day before Lent, is called Pancake Day in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot pancakes by landing flat with little forward speed; the flat batter cakes are the traditional Shrove Tuesday food.
